claim: FSDP's communication cost and per-GPU computation cost remain constant with respect to the number of GPUs, depending only on model and input sizes.
stance_target: the claim that at a fixed 1M-token global batch, adding GPUs shrinks per-GPU tokens and lets FSDP collectives dominate runtime
scope_conditions: FSDP training at fixed model and input size; strong-scaling regime
quoted_support: expected since the communication cost of FSDP and the computation cost per GPU remain constant with respect to the number of GPUs, depending only on the model and input sizes.

claim: As GPU count rises at fixed global batch, fewer tokens are assigned per GPU per iteration and FSDP communication (parameter AllGather plus gradient ReduceScatter) comes to dominate runtime.
stance_target: the claim that a 5-GPU box running a 1M-token global batch (200k tokens/GPU) is far from the comm-bound regime that large clusters hit
scope_conditions: Strong scaling at 16M-128M-token global batches, up to 10K GPUs
quoted_support: However, as the GPU count continues to increase, fewer tokens are assigned per GPU per iteration, causing FSDP communication---including parameter AllGather and gradient ReduceScatter---to dominate runtime.

claim: FSDP scales linearly with a 120M-token global batch up to 10K GPUs and delivers a 3.4x throughput gain from 1K to 8K GPUs at a 16M-token global batch.
stance_target: the claim that large global batches are the regime where FSDP scales well, so a 1M-token batch on 5 GPUs is comfortably inside the linear regime
scope_conditions: H800 cluster, 8 GPUs per node, 400 GB/s NVLink; 120M-token and 16M-token global batches
quoted_support: veScale-FSDP scales linearly with a 120M-token global batch up to 10K GPUs, while still delivering a 3.4x throughput gain from 1K to 8K GPUs at a 16M-token global batch.

claim: veScale-FSDP achieves 5-66% higher throughput and 16-30% lower memory usage than existing FSDP systems while scaling to tens of thousands of GPUs.
stance_target: the state of the art in FSDP implementation efficiency, which sets the ceiling for what sharding overhead can be engineered away
scope_conditions: Dense and sparse LLMs across scales; H800 cluster
quoted_support: veScale-FSDP enables zero-copy FSDP communications and natively supports block-wise quantization and non-element-wise optimizers, achieving 5~66% higher throughput and 16~30% lower memory usage than existing FSDP systems, while scaling efficiently to tens of thousands of GPUs.

claim: veScale-FSDP trains 2.4T-parameter models on only 1K GPUs without MFU degradation.
stance_target: the memory headroom that full sharding provides at scale, versus the 5-GPU box's much smaller shard group
scope_conditions: 1K H800 GPUs, 8K training tokens per GPU, 400B-2.4T parameters
quoted_support: Enabled by efficient memory management of DBuffer, veScale-FSDP can train 2.4T-parameter models on only 1K GPUs without any performance degradation.

claim: Existing FSDP implementations have distinct inefficiencies: DeepSpeed ZeRO suffers fragmented AllGathers, PyTorch FSDP1 has slow ReduceScatter, FSDP2 pays tensor-copy overhead, and Megatron-FSDP pays padding cost.
stance_target: the claim that FSDP's 1.5x communication multiplier is a floor, and real implementations can be worse
scope_conditions: Comparison of FSDP implementations as of 2026
quoted_support: DeepSpeed ZeRO pioneered FSDP research but suffers from fragmented AllGather operations and inefficient memory management. PyTorch FSDP1 addresses some AllGather inefficiency, but incurs slow ReduceScatter and does not solve memory overhead. PyTorch FSDP2 improves memory management but introduces a high tensor copy overhead.

claim: Unaligned communication buffers slow collectives, and the paper cites NCCL all-gather bandwidth measurements across byte alignments and protocols.
stance_target: the claim that collective efficiency depends on message-size alignment, relevant to whether bf16 compression hooks actually deliver 2x on a small ring
scope_conditions: NCCL all-gather with different byte alignments and protocols
quoted_support: Meanwhile, both FSDP1 and FSDP2 suffer from slow collectives due to unaligned communication buffers.

claim: Disabling the zero-copy DBuffer drops throughput to 92.8%, and disabling the planning algorithm drops it to 65.4%, showing most of the realized speedup comes from communication buffering rather than sharding format.
stance_target: the claim that communication-path engineering, not sharding math, dominates FSDP throughput
scope_conditions: 32 GPUs, GPT-OSS-style model with 8-bit Adam; component ablation
quoted_support: Table 2 shows that DBuffer and the planning algorithm account for most of the realized speedups: disabling them reduces throughput to 92.8% and 65.4%, respectively.

claim: Practical guidance is to avoid excessively large FSDP group sizes and use hierarchical parallelism (HSDP) to scale to larger GPU counts.
stance_target: the claim that a 5-GPU flat group is the right sharding scope for this box, since it is far below the group sizes where HSDP becomes necessary
scope_conditions: Large GPU clusters; FSDP group-size selection
quoted_support: Based on Figure 11 and our experience, a practical guideline is to avoid excessively large FSDP group sizes and use hierarchical parallelism (e.g., HSDP) to scale to larger GPU counts.

claim: The veScale-FSDP testbed is 8x H800 per node with 979 BF16 TFLOPS, 80 GB HBM and 400 GB/s NVLink, so its throughput numbers assume a fabric orders of magnitude faster than PCIe Gen2 x4.
stance_target: the transferability limit of these FSDP scaling results to the CMP 170HX box
scope_conditions: H800 cluster, 400 GB/s NVLink per GPU
quoted_support: each node contains 8xH800 GPUs (979 BF16 TFLOPS, 80 GB HBM) and 400 GB/s NVLinks.
